en: A Brief Preface to the Re-engraved *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra):

"The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the wondrous medicine for the opportune moment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual transformations. When patients encounter it, there are none whose ailments are not instantly cured.
Formerly, Ānanda manifested defilement and Daṅgā manifested lust; this was because they belonged to the class of those who perceive through form and hear through sound."
Because they were unable to sever the net of craving through a single expedient means, Ānanda initiated [the request] and the Tathāgata preached this sutra.
At that time, the assembly of holy ones in the gathering all saw emanated Buddhas emerge from within the Tathāgata’s crown-mark (uṣṇīṣa), seated upon jeweled lotuses and expounding divine mantras.
When these cut away their pure views, the flow was severed and no longer followed the sense-faculties.
Dust flows and can be cut off; this solid divine elixir is contained within the ten fascicles of the text.

I have once deliberated with my fellow practitioners on this sutra, yet seeking it in the original text yielded nothing, nor did seeking it in the commentaries of various masters yield anything—like gazing out at the ocean and seeing only its vastness.
It was only when I happened to obtain the *Jieshi Jueliu* (The Precept Master’s Cutting Off the Flow) and read it that I suddenly attained awakening. The physician then [acted] for himself.

What need is there for a physician to seek a physician elsewhere? It is like a king of physicians who, when afflicted by illness, abandons his own divine elixir to seek out other prescriptions and medicines;
how can such a person be called wise? Now that this "Cutting Off the Flow" has been brought forth, those harboring doubts will be like snow melted by boiling water.
Even those with wisdom would not abandon the ocean to recognize only a floating bubble. This matter is no small one; I wish to have it carved once again onto printing blocks.

Circulate this so that it flows like a stream; though one seeks to intercept it, it flows all the more. Readers should possess the "single eye" to obtain a single grain of divine elixir within the light of formlessness.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Jia-Yin year of the Wanli era by Shengxing of Puti Hermitage at Yuxi, with humble prostrations.
A Brief Preface to the *Lengyan jieliu* (The Lankavatara Sutra:
Cutting Off the Stream). The Tathagata takes formlessness as his form and non-speaking as his speech;

yet Ananda, arising from a perception of the Tathagata’s superior forms and arising from hearing the Tathagata’s Dharma-sound, pursues color and sound, causing his mind and eyes to flow and revolve. Thus was the case with Matangi.
When the woman saw [the Buddha], Sāṃvarī cast a spell upon her, binding her into the same single flow of transmigration.

Thus, the Tathāgata emitted a jewel-light from his crown, and emanated Buddhas who preached mantras and clarifications; by means of the markless mark, they severed her perception of marks, and by means of the unspeakable speech, they severed her hearing of sounds.
What stream could not enter? What stillness did not manifest? The ten-fascicle scripture was thus fully complete.

In this world, there are now dozens, even hundreds of schools that interpret the scriptures; furthermore, from the notion of "arising from non-existence" comes the doctrine of "arising from non-existence," and from "non-existence" comes the discourse on "existence"—the flow of textual exegesis has run wild and overflowed, turning the medicine of Ānanda into the illness of the Tathāgata.

Only the Dharma Master Jie alone raised the *uṣṇīṣa* upon his head as an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and by fusing and interpreting the scriptural texts, he finally cut off these myriad currents. Alas!
The nature is a vast, profound ocean; how could the feet of an elephant of fragrance ever cut across its current?
I still recall the year of Yiwu (1615), when the Dharma Master filled the hall at West Lake for a ceremony of releasing living beings (*fangsheng*), and we all recited this sutra together.

At the conclusion, the Precept Master emerged with several thousand words, his voice clear and resonant, his spiritual intent swift and penetrating. At that time, Grand Master Lianchi, Feng Kaizhi, Zhang Ruyuan, and Yu... [text fragment]... were present.

The eminent lay practitioners Changru and Sengru, seated among the assembly, all clapped their hands in appreciation and sighed in admiration. Yet those who had previously delivered the discourse now withdrew from their seats and hid themselves;
midway through, they nearly fell into the stream. Thereupon he reflected: "Reading ten thousand words on cutting off the flow is not equal to hearing a thousand words from a direct exposition.
If that is so, how much more so is it when reading the ten volumes of the Tathāgata’s definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) compared to once reaching the summit of realization?
The manifestation of these signs is indeed the meaning of "cutting off the stream"; this is yet another proof.

Written by the junior member of the Hulin Society, Zheng Zhihui, at the foot of Mount Huiri during the summer of the Wuxu year of the Wanli era, as a preface to the *Lengyan Jieliu* (The Lankavatara Sutra:
Cutting Off the Stream).

Now, wondrous enlightenment is not something that flows from the ocean; from where could it come? Meditation is fundamentally without cultivation—what meaning is there in speaking of "cutting off"? Alas!
In this age of semblance, among those who study the Buddha, the karmic legacy of wisdom is easily established, yet the habitual tendencies of desire are difficult to restrain.

Therefore, the Sūtra specifically cites Nanda as a mirror. At that time, Nanda was preeminent among those of vast learning; yet he was unable to reflect back upon the nature of his own essence to clarify it.
It precedes stillness yet pursues that which clings to limpidity; it follows the emergence of consciousness and gallops after one's own views and hearing.
It indulges in the sounds and colors of the Buddha. Prajñā says: "All that has marks is entirely illusory. Ānanda did not yet understand this; how could he have liberated himself from Dēṅgā?
Therefore, the Buddha did not merely display the crown-mark of invisibility; he used verbal teachings as his instruction. Otherwise, it would not be so.

How many layers of overflowing erudition are required! As for investigating the mind and discerning the views, extensively expounding the three categories and seven elements, and even reaching the ultimate convergence with the *tathāgatagarbha*—wherein [subject and object] are non-dual and both speech and thought are utterly transcended—one establishes practice that is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) based on the ultimately firm understanding.
This is detailed through the realizations of all the sages, yet it is specifically attributed to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara at its inception.
Having entered the stream [of the path], one forgets the final goal as *nirvāṇa* manifests before one;

that which is called *nirvāṇa* is precisely the wondrous essence revealed by the Buddha-dharma, which is free from all views. Furthermore, how could it ever be expressed or demonstrated through words? Alas!

Since the various commentaries of past and present have neglected the Tathāgata’s silent indication, how can they hope to "forget the words" by means of the "image"? Having lost the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they rely on mere inference.

When wisdom’s benefit recedes and false discourses spread far and wide, such that one is lost in the distance with no way back, Master Jieshan cut off the current and could not help but compose this work.

Yet the Way is fundamentally thus. If practitioners can truly turn the source and return to it, suddenly causing their skulls to dry up completely, they will then move freely through the two flows of birth-and-death and nirvana, whether in accordance with or contrary to them; such a person is a fragrant elephant.
There is no room for artifice; what could it mean to speak of "the hare and the horse"?
Inscribed by the Layman Taiyi, Jin Xuezeng, on the first volume of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, titled "Cutting the Stream."
Narrated by the later-day Tiantai śramaṇa Chuǎnrú.

The "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" refers to the manifestation of the supernatural transformations of Śākyamuni, the Great Awakened One. Using symbols to convey the meaning is the universal practice of the holy teachings.
Herein, Ānanda was immersed in a house of lust, and the great assembly desired to hear the essential points of the Dharma; thus, the World-Honored One, endowed with great majestic power...
Though he possessed the power [to act], his hand did not reach out to assist; though he was fully endowed with great *dharmapratisaṃvid* (eloquence), his mouth did not yet open to speak.

Then, from within his *uṣṇīṣa*, there surged forth light of a hundred jewels, and an emanation of the Buddha proclaimed a divine mantra. This signifies that both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are supreme, manifesting the simultaneous perfection of form and sound.
It sweeps away the illusory cataracts of seeing and hearing, such that the Great Purpose of this Sūtra is revealed without remainder.

That which excels both the Exoteric and Esoteric: the Sūtras are exoteric and the mantras are esoteric; the *Guhyagarbha* (Heart Essence) is non-dual and undifferentiated from the Heart [of the Buddha];
the *Uṣṇīṣa* (Crown Protuberance) is the sign of the Unsurpassed; and the Sūtras are the discourse of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Because the Esoteric encompasses the Exoteric and fully manifests within the *Uṣṇīṣa*, it is said to excel both. That which is sublime in both form and sound: the transformation Buddhas of the crown-light are the "form beyond form," the manifestation of form.
The Buddha’s incantations are sounds beyond sound; since both form and sound transcend the realm of conceptual thought, they are called "sublime.
Those with impaired vision and hearing perceive floating dust and illusory transformations, clinging to false appearances.

Failing to understand all of this, they give rise to deluded grasping, which obstructs the eye of pure wisdom and blocks the fundamental root of perfect penetration. Therefore, the practitioner said: "I..."
Seeing that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks were supremely wonderful and peerless, he yearned for them with longing and followed the Buddha to shave his head.
Yet it is also said: "I have awakened to the Buddha's manifested sounds of the Dharma; now, with my conditioned mind, I truly gaze upon him.
Is this not one who seeks Bodhi by chasing after forms and sounds? Once attached to form and sound, one's original clarity becomes obscured—just as was the case with Dēng-ga.

How could one not seize the opportunity? Why is this so? Because the Buddha-body and the female body are identical in their characteristics; the Buddha’s vision and the woman’s vision are identical in their sentiments.

Ānanda alone harbored resentment because he had personally touched her body, which became an obstacle created by Māra. He had not yet realized that the attachment to superior forms is the root cause of calamity.
Truly, she was a procuress who, while in the room, left him in a state of bewildered ignorance; moreover, he relied upon his great learning [to justify his lapse].

That such wisdom could have been encompassed by the ancient Brahmanic mantras surely has its own reason. Now, by manifesting the transformation-Buddhas from the Buddha’s crown, one knows that the forms of the thirty-two marks are not forms;
and by the transformation-Buddhas preaching the mantras, one knows that the sounds of the four unhindered eloquences are not sounds.
From this, one awakens to the realization that the dharmas of the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and the seven great elements are none other than the Tathāgatagarbha.

In the midst, phenomena manifest according to karma; because following karma is itself the nature, they are not existent. Because the nature follows karma, they are not empty. To be detached from both existence and non-existence—this is neither identity nor difference.

Thus, truth and falsehood are mutually fused, and all conceptual proliferation is severed. Regarding the cultivation and realization within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there is no longer any secret essential.
To see this is true seeing; to hear this is true hearing. At that very moment, the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) radiates its light. Ten thousand... [phenomena]... [arise].
At the conclusion of the *Xiàng* (The Elephant), the full title is given as: *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Śītātapatrā, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions*.

To take this as a mere prose text and offer various elaborate commentaries would likely not reflect the intention of the Supreme Sage in manifesting these signs to secretly benefit those with sharp faculties;
it is like the various light-manifestations in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which symbolize the various stages (*bhūmi*).

This Dharma-gate briefly follows the example of one sutra; all that can be understood through the text—where Mañjuśrī takes the mantra to protect [the assembly] and evil spells are extinguished, and Ānanda and Ḍākinī return to the Buddha’s presence—is precisely because when true wisdom functions, the deeds of Māra cease. The introduction concludes.
From here in the sutra text down to the middle of the fourth fascicle, it specifically relies on the essence of nature (*dharmatā*) to harmonize the myriad dharmas, clarifying them as such.
The coming of the secret cause is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, namely the prior realization of the Vairocana Dharma-realm; from the fourth fascicle to the end of the scripture,

it fully reveals the cultivation based on the nature to verify the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas, which is what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by the subsequent cultivation of the gateway to Samantabhadra’s practices.
*Śūraṅgama* translates as "Ultimate Solidity. The teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of this sutra are all ultimate;
thus, it is called a definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) text. There are five types of titles, which shall be explained in detail later.

When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated and wept with grief because he realized his precept-body was nearly destroyed by Dhaṇga, and that much learning had not benefited his power of the Path. People may encounter such a situation and remain complacent.
That being so, the wondrous scripture of the Śūraṅgama has nothing from which it is initiated, and the flowing stream of birth-and-death desire has nothing by which it is obstructed.

How could the manifestation of traces by those of great authority not be unconditioned? When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain the realization of Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—where "wondrous" (*miao*) signifies the esoteric (*mi*)—these terms such as *śamatha* refer to the causal conditions. Although the title is summarized in reverse order, it merely indicates the esoteric.

In response to this request for the Dharma, it must be explained in detail that there are three distinct types of *śamatha*: *samatha* is the state of profound stillness and tranquility; *samādhi* is the state of vast, perfect illumination;
and *dhyāna* is the non-duality of stillness and illumination. While they differ in their functional applications, their essence is eternally one.

Because these three and the one are perfectly interfused, they are called "wondrous. This is the seed-wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*) of all Buddhas and the spiritual awareness of every person. Thus it is said in a sutra: [One sutra...]
The "Principle" (zong) is that which can manifest [the essence], and this is called the "Secret Cause"; the "Essence" (ti) is that which is manifested, and this is called the "Treasury Nature.
Since the Principle and the Essence originally have no divergent paths, how could the cause and the fruit not be of one accord?

Therefore, in the subsequent text, sometimes two are cited to encompass three, or the Principle is cited to include the Essence. As for what the translators did not translate, its profound and brilliant elucidation depends upon the individual.
The "ear" is the primary expedient, the gateway for entering *samādhi*. This gateway has two distinctions: the general and the specific.
After Ānanda had realized the *garbha-citta* (the heart-mind of the treasury) in four fascicles, he requested:

"I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; I must enter through its doors. The World-Honored One then showed him the initial stage of awakening.

Although the meaning of the two determinations of the mind shows the relative superiority and inferiority of the six sense organs to enable entry through a single gate, it does not yet specifically point out which gate is essential.
Therefore, when [Ānanda] separately requested the fundamental organ of perfect penetration, the Buddha had the various sages each describe their own realization;

this then generally clarified that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), as well as the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), are all gates for entering the Way. Only [the teaching on] sound...
I have specially received the Imperial Edict to follow after the various sages and point toward the Avalokiteśvara who realized this verse, which says:
"The true essence of the teaching in this land is purity found in hearing sounds; those who wish to enter samādhi must truly do so by entering through hearing.

I pray that you will bestow your grace upon the future, so that they may be without doubt regarding this gate, and that it may be used to instruct Ānanda and others sinking in the delusions of the final age. Thus, the scripture is transmitted through the ear.
It is beyond doubt that the faculty of hearing as the perfect penetration (*śrotra-āyatana-pariśuddhi*) is the primary expedient, and it is fit to be taught to Ānanda.
For while Ānanda accumulated the habit of hearing to form a fault, Avalokiteśvara cultivated the habit of hearing to form a virtue;

the difference between merit and transgression lies solely in whether one follows the sound or enters the stream. Now, this reveals the Great Being’s fundamental, wondrous, and perfect faculty for the sake of those who have heard much.

The secret essence of initial cultivation is to ensure that one does not lose the original steps, so that the Great Function manifests before one—just as one who has fallen from the ground must rise back up from the ground.
If one abandons this, how can they hear the causes of the esoteric teachings? If one abandons this, upon what can they rely to discuss the myriad practices?

Therefore, Ānanda reproached himself for his failure to fully perfect the power of the Way despite his extensive learning, and further recounted the origins of his initial resolve and the appearance of the signs; the World-Honored One then [responded].
To those who are deluded, he shows them this, saying: "All sentient beings, because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure luminosity—employ various false thoughts.
Because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic existence. This essence of pure luminous nature is that which is represented by the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa, transcending all discrimination.
To employ various false thoughts is to act according to the characteristics of causal attachment and desire."

Since there is no other method for curing this notion, it is said: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices and is the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate.

Although Ānanda previously requested that all three names be listed, only the name "samādhi" is mentioned here; by mentioning one, the other two are subsumed, as the essential substance of the entire doctrine is present therein.
The term *samādhi* is called the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" because these words, by means of their signification, encompass the esoteric and return it to the exoteric.
The title "Śūraṅgama" (*Shou Lengyan Wang*) reveals the ultimate, adamantine essence that is to be expounded—the one that is supreme among all things.

Since there is no function apart from this essence, it is said to be "fully endowed with the myriad practices. It is the path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend [samsara] by a single gate.
This is because through samādhi, the eternally abiding mind is revealed, and one returns to the perfection of Bodhi, where there is nothing to be attained; such is the state of all Buddhas.

Now, as for why the mind is called "eternally abiding": if it is eternally abiding, then there is nowhere it does not abide; since there is nowhere it does not abide, it cannot be said to "abide" in any particular place.
Yet, Ānanda, you calculate in terms of the internal, the external, and even up to the non-attached—how could such things possibly exist?
Observe this: when the Tathāgata emitted light from the gate of his face, shaking the realms of all Buddhas, disparate worlds merged into one;
though we stood afar, we heard as one. Thus, the seven locations were merely false limitations; directly beneath them, everything is vast and open.

The primordial, pure, and tranquil essence of Nirvana is fully present within oneself and does not reside in the Buddha. Ānanda still takes the mind that is capable of inference to be the true mind—is this not so?
Is it not that by mistaking a thief for one's own son, one has lost what is called the tranquil and eternal nature of the mind?
From this, precious light once again surged forth from the *svastika* mark, reaching as far as the Tathāgatas of every atom and pervading Ānanda and the great assembly without exception.

Knowing that delusory objects cannot obstruct the light of wisdom, how could the wondrous mind differ from the eye of the Way? This reaches the point of entrusting a blind man with the task of discernment.
The lamp illuminates the clear identity of the mind and the eye, causing Dignāga to describe the wondrous nature of the adventitious dust and the eternal substrate;
Ānanda realizes that the hand’s opening and closing is like the guest, while the seeing that neither expands nor contracts is like the host;
the head’s shaking is like the dust, while the seeing that remains unmoved is like space. Thus, the Tathāgata’s light is entrusted to Dignāga.
Just as [the Buddha] awakened Ānanda by using Ānanda himself to reprove those present in the assembly, he said:
"If you further say that what moves is called 'dust' and what does not abide is called 'guest,' I reprove the assembly for their failure to realize the immovability within movement.
Thus he said: "Observe, Ānanda: it is your head that moves; the seeing has no movement, yet the hand has opening and closing."

When seen as a whole, there is neither expansion nor contraction; why then do you now become deluded regarding the Lord who is quiescent and eternal, taking motion for your body and motion for your environment—is this not the loss of the true nature of mind?

By pursuing the turbid adventitious dust of agitation, from beginning to end, you undergo birth and extinction in every thought-moment—is this not identifying external objects as the self? The nature that is quiescent and eternal has been present from the very beginning.
Because I was deluded by it and turned my back upon it, I am said to be in saṃsāra, flowing and wandering within it through my own doing.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, spoke of their own awakening; they had thus attained thorough understanding.

This is the meaning of the guest-dust and the host-space. If one can truly awaken to this, then regarding the body and mind—whether true or false, empty or real—and their present arising and ceasing, as well as non-arising and non-ceasing, what further doubt could there be? However, the reason Ānanda was able to awaken was twofold:
first, he was pressed by the World-Honored One; second, he relied on Cīrṇa’s words. This precisely refers to relying on others for understanding and reflecting inwardly.

Because you are still deluded, I pray that you will clarify these two meanings so as to bring them to light. Furthermore, regarding the King of Videha’s description of the unchanging vision when observing the river:

although this belongs to the "seeing-essence" (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*), its substance is fundamentally true; it is simply the aforementioned vision of the original radiance, which is inherently devoid of motion or stillness.
To realize that the substance of this vision is fundamentally without motion or stillness is like understanding that the Buddha’s hand is fundamentally without being upright or inverted.

There is no correct or inverted state, yet from the very moment of inversion, there is neither arising nor ceasing, and yet arising and ceasing manifest; as arising and ceasing arise, the illuminating nature is lost.
Therefore it is called "dark obscurity. This very dark obscurity becomes emptiness and form; form is intermingled with delusive thoughts, and thus the body of the five aggregates is fully present.
Thus, the faculties are separated from their objects and wisdom is clouded by emotions; even though one may receive the teachings of the Tathāgata...
Thus, when this Dharma-sound manifests, one contemplates it with a mind of conditions; since this mind exists only by depending on forms and sounds, it is not a permanent master.
Therefore, the World-Honored One further points to the moon outside to demonstrate the nature that does not return.

By expanding the mind’s vision to equalize things, self, and others, and by tearing down the barriers of truth and falsehood, right and wrong, one directly reaches the wondrous, pure, eternal, and omnipresent state.
Because this is the realm of ultimate reality, he offers this verse in response to Mañjuśrī:

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, while abiding in samādhi, perceive both the seer and the objects of seeing, as well as all imagined forms, to be like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be within them 'is' or 'is not'? Tell me now, when you observe this seeing..."

The various manifestations of sensory objects are called delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*). One cannot transcend these within them as either "is" or "is not" because one is deluded about oneself and pursues external objects, causing "is" and "is not" to arise alternately.
It is precisely because this true, essential, wondrously enlightened nature of clarity manifests that it can cause you to transcend the pointing at "is" and "is not";
this is because one realizes that objects are identical to the mind, and thus both "is" and "is not" are simultaneously extinguished. The above is the general summary.
The answer was merely to clarify for Ānanda the nature of the two—reality and falsehood—as manifested within body and mind.
Ānanda said, "Truly, as the Dharma King has taught, the nature of awareness that pervades the ten directions is profoundly still and eternally abiding; its nature is neither arising nor ceasing.
This was his realization of the principle explained above: that the seeing-nature is constant and pervasive, beyond both "is" and "is not. He then spoke of what was discussed with Śābika...
Regarding the difference between the *tattva* (ultimate truth) and the "true self" (*ātman*) asserted by various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) as being all-pervasive throughout the ten directions:

it is because the calculations of the Brahmins are confused with the truth that they must be distinguished. Although Ānanda has corrected the error of the non-Buddhists regarding spontaneity (*svabhāva*), he does not realize that his own grasping at causes and conditions is likewise mistaken;
for the clarity and brilliance of his awareness see that, fundamentally, there is neither light nor darkness.

Because it fills all that can exist within space, it cannot be said that it perceives this by depending on that. Furthermore, you should know that when one sees seeing, that seeing is not "seeing" itself;
this means that true seeing is not only apart from the four types of external objects of the physical sense-organ, but is also apart from the essence of the clarity of seeing.
Since even this essence of seeing must be discarded, what more remains to be said?

He said: "If even the seeing of seeing has already departed from the essence of seeing such that seeing cannot reach it, why do you further speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of combination?

Ānanda, his confusion and distress increased all the more at this. This was because the "seeing of seeing" had already advanced beyond the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*), and the "awakening of awakening" had begun to depart from the cataract of awakening.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first raised the example of the shadow of a cataract—a localized affliction easily understood by all—to illustrate the point.
Because it opens up the vision that has been difficult to comprehend throughout the accumulation of kalpas of joy, it says: "Take you as an example today;
with your eyes you perceive mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings—all of these are produced by the disease of vision from beginningless time.

Yet, since you are able to realize that this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are entirely illusory, how could you ever be ultimately overwhelmed by what is illusory? Therefore, it is said: 'Awakened to what is seen...'"
To perceive the cataract is to perceive that which is not the cataract; only when one transcends the cataract through perception does one know that the cataract is illusory.

Therefore it is said: "This is truly the seeing of seeing. Why then do you further clarify "awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing"? This is to reprimand those who have not yet realized that the present body and mind are fundamentally like flowers in the sky, having no actual substance as the essence of the seeing of seeing. If that were the true essence of seeing, it would not even be called "seeing."
What is called "seeing" is that which can be seen; the seer itself cannot be seen. It is said, "The entire earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa"—one who knows this speaks truly.

From here on, whether in identity or distinction, they are interwoven and fully revealed, successively expanded and propagated, so as to cause one to realize that within the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, all phenomena whatsoever are empty and illusory. Therefore, it is said: "Taking Jambudvīpa as an analogy."
"Ananda, extend this even to all conditioned lands and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions; they are all of one and the same enlightened, luminous, untainted, and wondrous mind.
Their seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise falsely through the conjunction of conditions for delusion, and they die falsely through the conjunction of conditions for delusion.

Yet, because there exists the false cause of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, there consequently arises the false condition of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world. Thus, through the conjunction of causes and conditions,"

All false conceptualizations of birth and death are vast and infinite; if one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then the causes of birth and death will be extinguished.
The nature of Bodhi is unborn and undying, its pure and wondrous essence—the fundamental awakening—is eternally abiding.
Alas, Ānanda, because your doubts regarding conjunction have not yet ceased, the World-Honored One speaks again.

To explain this by means of four meanings and further elaborate upon its various characteristics, the intent is to ensure that all mental attachments are completely dispelled and all phenomena are analyzed without omission.
"The various illusory manifestations of the floating dust arise where they are and perish where they are" means that as soon as something arises, it simultaneously perishes.
"Illusory falsehoods are called 'characteristics'" means that objects lack any reality corresponding to their names; in truth, there is only the One.

Because it is real, its nature is said to be the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity. It is truly said that my own learning has never reached this level; I merely offer this as an introduction. Regarding the phrase "entering the stream and losing the object" within the context of hearing:

for an ordinary person, the ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness, which constitutes "hearing," while the hearing-consciousness rushes toward external objects, which constitutes "streaming. Now, when Avalokiteśvara contemplates and listens, he causes [the consciousness] to enter back [into the faculty];
hence it is called "entering the stream. Because he can extinguish sound and perfect his hearing, it is called "losing the object. This refers to the aforementioned sound.

Regarding "the dusts below" (dusts under the feet): entering the stream means that because the internal [mind] subdues the external dusts, they are naturally extinguished; thus it is said, "that which is entered is itself quiescent.

When the two marks of movement and stillness are clearly seen not to arise, and this gradually increases until "what is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted," this is because one has attained the wondrously wondrous hearing-mind, wherein the essence of the mind leaves behind all hearing.
Therefore, it is called "exhaustion. This is what was previously referred to as "this faculty first being resolved, one first attains..."
The person is empty, yet one perceives that hearing has an end; because this very "end" is itself non-ending, it is said that "hearing does not abide in its ending.

When that which perceives is empty of what is perceived, the emptiness-nature becomes perfectly luminous, forming the liberation of dharmas. When the perception of emptiness is perfectly complete, that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished;
this means that even the emptiness of the perception of emptiness is empty—what is called the non-arising of mutual emptiness. As for arising and ceasing, they are external.
The sense organs within the realm of dust, as well as consciousness and the mind—all delusions and karmic actions—are termed phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.

Now, because they are all entirely empty, it is said that they have "already ceased. Since they have already ceased, they do not cease again; therefore, it is called "quiescent cessation" (*śānta-nirodha*).

The more they cease, the more they manifest; this is called "manifest presence. The more they transcend, the more they are identical; thus, they harmonize upward with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Sharing the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata, he enters all lands through thirty-two manifestations;
below, he unites with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrow and longing as all beings.

He bestows the fourteen kinds of fearlessness, extending his blessings to all sentient beings, and manifests many wondrous forms capable of preaching boundless divine mantras—all of these being devoid of any self-referential basis.

The concluding summary of the profound clarity and vast illumination attained through the "Hearing-Remnant" (Śruti-śeṣa) states: "When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that I follow the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination;
by gaining mastery over the conditioned mind, I entered the aspect of the 'flow' and attained Samādhi, thereby accomplishing Bodhi—this is the foremost.

Some may doubt this, for how could a Bodhisattva of the Thirty-two Manifestations appear in the form of a Buddha, or how could the Fourteen Fearlessnesses involve sinking into or departing from [samsara]?

The afflictions of body and mind pervade the vast and boundless Dharma-realm; the manifestations of numerous hands and eyes are all symbolic expressions of the Dharma, never having been realized as substantial entities.
Alas! Is this not a case of creating obstacles for oneself while disregarding that perfect penetration?

One should know that Avalokiteśvara is the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna (Righteous Dharma Radiance); why then dwell solely upon the traces of his responses, when sentient beings are capable of evoking his compassion?
If one follows the Way, what difficulty is there in parting from the suffering of illusion and delusion? Bending and rising again, one soothes the four seas;

moreover, through the cognition of causal conditions, body and mind mutually pervade the ten directions. This is the beginning of the wondrousness of transcending hearsay. When a fish becomes a dragon, its head and horns become distinct;
when a person ascends to sagehood, their hands and eyes are truly divine. Do not look out at the vast ocean in bewilderment or remain confined by narrow prejudices; please attend to this practice.
Entering the stream, one loses the locus of perception; yet one must still rely on the radiant brilliance of Great Compassion to be shown once and for all one's original face.

Only then does one believe that the words and realizations of the Sages are beyond deception. Now, as the various Sages have each set forth their methods of perfect penetration, the World-Honored One emitted light from his five limbs, which traveled afar to drench the countless Tathāgatas.
Those countless Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs, which came [to meet it].
The pouring of water upon the Buddha’s crown symbolizes that the ultimate fruit of pure and extreme radiance is shared by all.

That the Bodhisattvas and Arhats of both that realm and this land likewise have their crowns sprinkled with light signifies the mutual fusion of cause and effect; every teaching presented and every realization attained is unsurpassed.
That the forest trees and ponds all proclaim the sounds of the Dharma, and that jewel lights interlace like a net of precious threads, is a sign of faith.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth are none other than the Tathāgatagarbha; they are none other than wondrous adornments.

Because this is a rare and auspicious omen, it causes all beings to universally attain the Vajrasamādhi. Through the swiftness of severing delusions by means of the Vajra-like Samādhi, one immediately attains the rank of the true cause of the first stage (Prathamabhūmi).
Because one has stepped upon this true position, even the heavens respond with various auspicious omens. This is the truth.
Because the ten realms are fully manifested within causal wisdom, they constitute one hundred realms;

thus, the rain of hundred-jeweled lotuses—intermingled and variegated in blue, yellow, red, and white—represents the gradual and successive entry into the stages of abiding, practice, direction, and ground, whether by skipping or following the sequence.
That the voids of the ten directions take on the color of the seven treasures signifies the realization of the seven eternal fruits from within the essence of quiescent extinction.
Entering the universal gateway of perfect penetration, habitual outflows are eternally eliminated, and there is no longer any separation between the environment and its inhabitants;
therefore, the mountains and rivers of this Sahā world simultaneously cease to appear, and the lands within a single mote of dust merge to form one realm.

That the chanting of *brahman* hymns and songs is spontaneously performed signifies that for those who have realized entry into this state, the sounds of the Dharma are all like this. This concludes the gateway of perfect penetration.
Thereupon the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "Observe now these great bodhisattvas and arhats, each of whom has spoken of the expedient means for their initial attainment of the Way.
In their actual practice, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority;
this is because the nature of the sages is such that nothing is not penetrated. Because there is nothing that is not penetrated, such auspicious omens have been manifested. I now wish—"
He commanded Ānanda to awaken to the twenty-five modes of practice: "Who among them is suited to the faculties of this world’s sentient beings after my parinirvāṇa?

Through which gate of skillful means can they easily achieve success? Mañjuśrī, receiving this decree, selected only the faculty of hearing; this is what is meant by being "specifically suited to the occasion.
The verse states: "The nature of the ocean of enlightenment is limpid and perfect; its limpid perfection is the primordial source of enlightenment."

"Sublime" refers to what was previously stated: "the nature-awareness is subtly luminous, and fundamental awareness is luminously sublime. This is intended to select the faculty for perfect penetration;

first, it establishes the essence of perfect penetration by employing the single character "ocean," through which the meaning of "entering the stream" becomes apparent. The subsequent statement, "by reversing the flow, one attains non-delusion," is rooted in this.
As for the phrase "fundamental luminosity shines forth and produces objects," "fundamental luminosity" refers to the originally sublime, wondrous awareness.
"Brilliance" (ming) arises from the original brilliance and is falsely manifested as that which is illuminated; therefore it is called "that which is established.

Once that which is established and that which is illuminated have been set up, the true nature becomes obscured; therefore it is said that "the nature of illumination is lost. The "nature of illumination" refers to the true nature that gives rise to illumination.

Due to delusive confusion, there is empty space; because of space, the world is established. This means that the state of obscurity and darkness becomes "emptiness," and within this obscure darkness, the coagulation of darkness forms "form" (rūpa).

One might also consider that while the clarity [of the water] constitutes the land, the awareness [of it] constitutes the sentient beings; this is precisely because the various deluded thoughts regarding form cause the characteristics of thought to become the body.

For once there is a false basis for the distinction between the environment (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*), the essence of pure wondrousness can neither be made perfect nor made pervasive;
thus, a single delusion becomes the body, and one is certainly deluded into perceiving the physical body as being within oneself. Thus spoke Śūnyatā-utpanna.

Within Great Enlightenment, it is like a single bubble arising from the ocean; when the bubble vanishes, the emptiness was originally non-existent—how much more so the various realms of the three worlds?

This clarifies that the essence of enlightenment is fundamentally pervasive and unitary. Because it does not follow after sensory objects, the substance of perfect penetration is inherently boundless.

Thus, when purity reaches its ultimate limit, radiant penetration is attained, and tranquil illumination encompasses empty space. When a practitioner attains this, all objective realms are wondrous; therefore, they turn back to seek contemplation.
The world is like a dream; when one hears of the Buddhas, why does the Buddha not hear himself?
The "hearer" is the Buddha, and "Buddha" refers to the awakened nature (*bodhi*) spoken of by all Buddhas. This essence of awakening is my true hearing; it cannot be heard as an object.
How can that which is heard know the Buddha? Therefore, the *Sūtra* says: "O Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back your inverted faculty of hearing and listen inwardly to hear."

Ānanda, when the great assembly heard this instruction on the contemplation of the Buddha-bodhi and Great Nirvana—like a traveler far away who has not yet returned but clearly understands the road leading back home—the previous demonstration of the perfect penetration of the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) and the analysis of the fundamental source of perfect penetration merely clarified the origin of the practice; therefore, it was said that they only "knew the way. If...

Since one must prepare for the journey when intending to return home, [the text] requests that the rules for concentrating the mind be established and the site of practice (the *bodhimaṇḍa*) be set up;
this leads to the exposition of the fifty-five stages of true Bodhi, which precisely clarifies the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices.

The three—precept, concentration, and wisdom—are collectively termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), because the ocean of awakening within sentient beings is fundamentally perfect and limpid; it is only through attachment to this profound stillness that consciousness arises, flowing and scattering as it rushes toward external objects.
The objects of the senses are called outflows (*āsrava*); now, by relying on the pure discipline (*śīla*), one restrains body and mind so that they shine with inner clarity.

Within this, the samādhi of right concentration and the wondrous wisdom of perfect penetration are fully present. The Buddha has proclaimed the grave faults of each—lust, killing, stealing, and lying—calling them severe and definitive clear instructions.
Furthermore, he stated that if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyān; this is indeed the case.
The characteristics of the precepts are inherently easy to know and easy to understand, yet they constitute practices that are difficult to receive and difficult to maintain.

Since the root of suffering in saṃsāra and the wondrous, eternal state of peace and happiness both depend upon these, how can one not feel shame at death and dread it, when observing the Buddha’s earnest and urgent exhortations?
The seventh fascicle extensively elucidates the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s practice, instructing one to maintain the fourfold restraint as pure as ice and frost;

that one cannot produce any branches or leaves oneself is because, although the myriad practices are numerous, these constitute the root. If people today can indeed refrain from [deluded] conditions...

The demonic activities of form, fragrance, taste, and touch naturally dissolve; yet, alas, being drawn by the牵引 (attraction) of past habits, one’s mind is as equal to that of the Buddhas in the morning, but one’s conduct falls short of that of ordinary beings by evening.
The more one hears and sees, the more intense the delusions and karmic afflictions become.

Without relying on the power of divine mantras, there is ultimately no way to attain liberation. Herein it is clarified that establishing an altar and reciting mantras can enable one to realize the sacred fruit—this is the transformation.
The Buddha is the inconceivable Buddha; the mantra is the inconceivable Dharma; the maṇḍala is the inconceivable realm;

and the fellow practitioners of pure precepts are inconceivable persons. When such people give rise to such a mind, enter such a realm, and practice such a Dharma, they will certainly and without doubt obtain such a fruit.
Because the mantra possesses supreme benefit, the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, [protect it].
All ghosts and spirits vow to protect those who uphold [this teaching], so that they may be free from demonic obstacles.
In the final age, those who abandon the mantra-heart while discussing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* merely increase their erudition in vain; let the practitioner exert themselves.

Since the principles and practices have now been fully set forth above, if one does not open up the sacred stages (*āryabhūmi*), how can the signs of the realization of the fruit be manifested? As the first fascicle states: "The mind and speech are direct."
Therefore, from the beginning to the end, throughout the stages and their intervals, there are forever no signs of crookedness or deviation. Now it must be explained in detail; thus I ask:
what is called the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*)? From what point among the forty-four minds does one gradually attain the vision of practice?
To what place does one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)? And what is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)?

In the sequence of questions posed by Śāriputra, the stages are arranged in gradual order; this is because he first causes [the audience] to understand the three gradual stages so as to encompass all the positions.
When the Buddha was about to reveal the positions of the various sages, he first showed the two causes of delusion for sentient beings and the world:
because of the inversion of nature, when bodhi is transformed into afflictions, one becomes the twelve classes of living beings.
When the nature does not undergo inverted transformation, it turns birth-and-death into nirvana, thereby establishing the sixty stages of the sages;
this is the source of delusion and enlightenment and must be discerned. To state the essential point: the nature is the luminous primordial mind, from which a fleeting false luminosity arises.
Both that which covers and that which is covered are the root of non-abiding. This non-abiding establishes the world and all sentient beings. If one understands this...
When there is no abiding, one knows that the delusion has no basis and that the truth likewise does not exist as a single entity.

To desire to return to the truth is the root of perversion, from which the twelve classes of beings first arise. Therefore, the world exists because of movement; from sound to the six types of confused delusions, they constitute the nature of karma.
Thus, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this [delusion]. This clarifies the delusiveness of both the primary and secondary realms.
Woven together, these constitute the fundamental source from which the twelve categories of sentient beings arise.

Therefore, when the world’s sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles exhaust their twelve transformations and return to a single cycle, they recombine within the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). Here, the three periods of time and the four directions interpenetrate one another;
thus, the sentient beings who undergo transformation constitute the number twelve. Form, sound, odor, and taste are that which undergoes transformation.
The fundamental nature of the world is that the worlds revolve and interpenetrate one another, forming the number twelve; this "revolving" is precisely the meaning of "interpenetration.
As it says below: "Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted states, there is this world of egg-born beings and so forth.

Thus, one cannot exhaustively distinguish between the twelve transformations as the "transforming agent" (nengbian) or the "transformed object" (suobian). Each of the twelve classes of birth [is thus established].

Those who possess the twelve inversions do so because they mutually possess one another through the same single principle (*tathatā*). What Tiantai clarifies as "actualized" refers to the "factual creation" (*shizao*);
that which remains latent and submerged is "principle-endowment" (*lizhi*). This endowment has nothing further to be endowed, for it is entirely the single essence of awakening.
If one were to subsume this under the six stages of realization, it is what is called "identity with principle" (*lijie*), because all classes of living beings are identical with the Buddha.

One may advance in cultivation; upon hearing the principle once, it immediately becomes the "name" [stage]. Now, within these three gradual stages, one eliminates its auxiliary causes and hollows out its primary nature;
this belongs to the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*). Second, as the text itself states:

"With one's own physical body, without needing the divine eye, one naturally perceives the ten directions... up to the purity of past lives, attaining freedom from hardship and peril"; this belongs to... [the stage of true semblance].

The "Similar" stage is the third; it contradicts its own manifest karma and further clarifies the partial realization that follows upon the preceding two stages of "Observational Practice" (*vipaśyanā*) and "Similarity.

The text states: "Reversing the flow, they are entirely one, and the six functions do not operate"—this refers to the complete suppression of the five abodes [of ignorance], which is identical to the preceding stage of Observational Practice.
From "the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure" up to "all Tathāgatas' secret... [is the stage of Partial Realization].
That "the perfect, pure, and wondrous all appear within it" means that the afflictions of view and thought have already been severed, which is identical to the preceding stage of semblance.

That "this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" means that they have transcended from the ten stages of faith and entered the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), where the first layer of ignorance is broken;

this constitutes the stage of partial realization. From here, one gradually cultivates and establishes the ranks of the sages, referring specifically to the respective positions within the stage of partial realization.

The signs of advancement do not pertain directly to the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā). Combining the text concerning Dry Wisdom with what preceded it, it shares the same meaning as the previous descriptions:
the craving for desire is dried up, the faculties and their objects no longer correspond, the flow is reversed and unified, and the six functions cease to operate.

The grasping mind is void and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom; the nature of this wisdom is perfectly bright, illuminating the ten directions, identical to the description of the ten directions given previously.

Regarding the meaning of the land being "brightly pure and equal," if it refers to the state where the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have not yet been destroyed, it belongs to the phase of the "observational practice" (*kuan-hsing*) on the verge of completion;
if it refers to the state where the views and afflictions have already been destroyed, it is identical to the "conformable" (*xiang-si*) phase within the stage of the ten faiths (*shixìn*).

Since the "Dry Wisdom" (*gānhuì*) now stands prior to the ten faiths, it should be directly explained as belonging to the stage of observational practice. Accordingly, the Ten Fascicles [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*] states: "From..."

From this point onward, all stages—the ten faiths, ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayakīti*)—are without exception included within this diamond wisdom.

The fact that ordinary beings of the past inherently possess the state of sainthood is the "Identity in Principle" (*liri ji*). From this point, hearing [the teaching] constitutes the "Identity in Name" (*mingzi ji*);

the stage of Dry Wisdom (*ganhui*) is the "Identity in Practice" (*guanheng ji*); the ten stages of faith (*shixin*) are the "Identity in Similitude" (*xiangsi ji*); from the ten stages of faith up to Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*) is the "Identity in Partial Realization" (*fenzheng ji*);

and Wonderful Enlightenment (*miaojue*) is the "Ultimate Identity" (*jiujing ji*). Thus, the scripture begins with Dry Wisdom and culminates in Wonderful Enlightenment, constituting the twelve identities—both single and combined.
These are opened up individually according to their respective stages as "single" (dān), while each stage possessing all ten [factors] is called "compound" (pīṭha).

Thus, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds constitute five compounds; the Dry Wisdom, Heat, Peak, Patience, and World-First Dharma, along with the Sublime, constitute seven singles.
By counting these seven singles and five compounds, they total twelve. The explanation is as stated in the *Changshui* commentary on the Sūtra: "These various grounds are all..."
By means of the ten profound metaphors observed through the diamond-like *śamatha*, one employs various *vipaśyanā* to purify, realize, and gradually penetrate deeper into observation;

this "observation" (*vipaśyanā*) is another name for the mind. To be more precise, since both terms consist of two characters, it should also be said that upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one has begun to awaken and first attains the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*). This refers to the first and second stages of faith.

Regarding "consecration" (abhiṣeka): in India, all profound Vaipulya sūtras containing esoteric language are generally subsumed under the Consecration Section.

According to the specific context of this sūtra, it refers to the light rays emitted by the Buddhas mutually drenching the crowns of the heads [of the Bodhisattvas], as well as the water of wisdom for the Bodhisattvas' reception of office.
It is for this reason that it is called "Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*). In general, when Tiantai explains a title, he employs five levels of analysis:

name (*nāman*), essence (*svabhāva*), doctrine (*artha*), function (*kriyā*), and the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). Within the "name," there are further seven types: the three single [terms], the three compound [terms], and the one complete [title].

At the beginning of this sutra, the title is fully endowed with all three aspects: person, dharma, and metaphor. "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" refers to the person who transforms Buddhas; "Dhāraṇī-heart" refers to the dharma.
The Dharma is the metaphor for the Treasure Seal; the rest may be understood by analogy. This sutra takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) as its essence, as the scripture states:

"I desire to enable you all to penetrate the true reality. It takes subtle and secret contemplation as its primary principle (*śāstra*), clarifying the wondrous *śamatha* and other practices as the method for the realization of enlightenment by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because cause and effect are perfectly encompassed therein, it takes the destruction of delusion and the revelation of truth as its function.

It extensively elucidates that all phenomena are illusory to sever all delusions and karma, thereby revealing the eternally abiding true mind; thus, the Mahāyāna *Paya* (Cream) serves as its doctrinal characteristic.
This scripture begins with the eternal mind and culminates in the attainment of the ultimate fruit, being in kind similar to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

where "all obstacles are ultimate awakening," and "whether mindfulness or forgetfulness, there is nothing that is not liberation"—

If all that conforms [to this] constitutes a Dharma-gate, the Great Master Zhiyi remarked that while the *Avataṃsaka* still retains a dual character, this sutra is classified as belonging to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) and does not equal the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which is pure and unmixed. Following the explanation of this title, Ānanda and the great assembly were graced by the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Pañcara*.
This "Unsurpassed Treasure Seal," the meaning of which is the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, is expressed by the Buddha-peak divine mantra (*buddhoṣṇīṣa-vidyā*).
Since the titles of the Esoteric Sūtras are not uniform, it is said that they "simultaneously hear" the names and categories of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

This refers to the supreme subtle principle of the sudden awakening to *dhyāna* and the progressive cultivation of the stages of sainthood; it serves as a general conclusion regarding the benefits of the three phases of seeing, cultivation, and realization, and the severance [of afflictions].

thus, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teachings and their capacities may be known. Following the conclusion of the sutra’s main body, the auxiliary path will now be elucidated;

This refers to thoughts that transcend the ordinary; those such as Bao-lianxiang and others, having followed only evil karma, have all fallen into hell.
This passage enumerates the ten habitual practices and the six intersecting afflictions to fully clarify the various retributive sufferings and the characteristics of hell.

As for the three evil destinies and the human condition, although their suffering and joy differ, they are none other than the revolving cycle of birth and death.

It is said that these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this saṃsāra. Furthermore, it is said that when one minutely investigates the seven destinies, there is nothing but a state of delusion and ignorance throughout all modes of existence.

It is to cause those with signs of delusion to awaken to this conditioned nature, so that they may first attain the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). The preceding discussion on the seven destinies was intended to clarify the causes and effects across the three periods of time;
now, we shall examine in detail the cultivation within the present life to clarify the essential points regarding various demonic realms (*māra-viṣaya*).

The primary task is to thoroughly realize that body and mind are fundamentally empty, such that demons and Buddhas are of one essence. When a practitioner gives rise to various states during meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they must not grasp at them.
Thus, Māra is also the Buddha when one grasps at them, and the Buddha is also Māra when one grasps at them. As it says in the section on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*):
"This is merely a temporary attainment through the power of practice; it is not a realization of sainthood. If you do not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a 'wholesome state';

if you take it to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall under the sway of various demons. This is the essential principle regarding the objects of these aggregates. Regarding the major sections for aiding the path, it is stated in the first fascicle: [text follows].
Sentient beings, from time immemorial, possess various seeds of inverted karma that naturally cluster like *akṣa* berries;

Therefore, these many divergent paths are now closed, so that the true path may be ascended.

One who is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *śuklavipaśyanā* (dry wisdom) and perfect, luminous, refined mind, within which transformation arises like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli—

as well as the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine grounds (*bhūmi*) and the perfect luminosity of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), thereby entering the Tathāgata’s wondrously adorned [state].
The ocean of solemnity is perfected in Bodhi, returning to the state of non-attainment; since even Bodhi itself cannot be attained, how much less can other things reach this principle?
When the various maras cease of their own accord, one speaks of the mutual functioning [of the faculties], whereby one can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *kandha-hui* (dry wisdom).
This refers generally to adamantine wisdom and does not exclusively refer to the stage of dry wisdom prior to faith; therefore, it is said to be "like."

This indeed transcends the stages such as the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine stages (*vajra-daśabhūmi*) is finely analyzed," by examining the characters "transcend" (*chao*) and "practice" (*xing*), one knows that the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) penetrates through all positions; this is very clear.
